Automakers and charging companies only invest at full scale when the end date for gasoline car sales is certain, so a firm deadline is what makes the switch to electric cars happen.
Every gasoline car sold today will be on the road for many years, so the cheapest way to cut future emissions is to stop adding new ones.
Past safety and emissions standards were routinely called impossible when announced, and the industry usually found a way once the deadline was firm.
Long prison sentences generally do little to reduce crime compared with raising the odds of being caught.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether crime is prevented more by keeping known offenders locked away for longer or by making arrest more likely in the first place.

text: Most people who commit crimes do not expect to be caught, so the length of a sentence they never expect to serve does not enter their thinking.
Young men commit most crimes and stop on their own as they get older, so years added to the end of a sentence hold people who would have quit anyway.
Money spent on extra years in prison could instead hire investigators and patrol officers, which raises the chance of being caught and does change behavior.
A person in prison cannot commit crimes against the public, so every added year prevents whatever that person would have done outside.
A small number of repeat offenders commit a large share of all serious crime and keep at it well into middle age, so long sentences hold exactly the people who would not have quit on their own.
Being caught only deters people if what follows is serious, so more arrests paired with short sentences give offenders little to fear.
Judges should be allowed to keep suspects they consider dangerous in jail before trial, even when those suspects could afford bail.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether a judge's guess about future danger can justify locking up someone not yet convicted.

text: Someone arrested for a violent act and released the same day can go after the same victim or witness before the trial ever happens.
Bail based on money frees the wealthy and holds the poor, so a judgment about danger is fairer than a judgment about cash.
Public confidence in the courts falls when people see a suspect walk out hours after a serious arrest.
A person who has not been convicted is presumed innocent, and jailing that person is punishment before any trial.
Predicting who is dangerous is guesswork, and a judge facing public pressure will err toward holding people who would have caused no harm.
Even a few weeks in jail can cost a person their job, housing, and custody of their children, so detention harms whole families whether or not the charge holds up.
Governments should put protecting the environment ahead of economic growth when the two conflict.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether growth is the thing that damages the environment or the thing that eventually pays to repair it.

text: Damage to nature often cannot be undone, while lost growth can be made up later, so the cautious choice is to protect what cannot be replaced.
Growth that uses up resources is borrowed from future generations who never agreed to the loan.
Markets reward growth but give nobody a reason to pay for clean air, so when growth and clean air collide only a government rule keeps the air clean.
Countries that are clean today mostly got rich first and then paid for cleanup, so growth is the path to protection rather than its enemy.
Strict environmental limits in one country push dirty production to places with weaker rules, so the harm moves instead of shrinking.
Rules that put the environment ahead of growth raise prices and cut jobs for the people least able to absorb either.
Technology tends to solve environmental problems better than restrictions on how people live.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether clean technology arrives on its own or only because rules created a reason to build it.

text: Past resource scares tended to end with a new method or a new material, not with rationing, and there is no reason to expect the pattern to stop.
Restrictions on daily life are unpopular and get rolled back, while a cleaner option that is also cheaper stays adopted for good.
A rule freezes today's best answer in place, while innovation keeps finding better answers that the rule would have blocked.
New technology arrives on its own schedule while environmental damage is happening now, so waiting for a technical fix is a decision to accept that damage in the meantime.
New technology is often used to consume more rather than less, so efficiency gains get eaten by growth unless something limits the total.
The clean technologies that did succeed usually appeared because rules and targets made someone pay for them, so the restriction is what produces the invention.
Longer prison sentences generally make communities safer.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether the extra years are served by people who would have kept offending or by people who would have stopped anyway.

text: A person who is in prison cannot commit crimes on the street, and every year added is a year the community is protected from that person.
Adding years to a sentence raises the price of getting caught, and a higher price makes some people decide the crime is not worth it.
A few repeat offenders account for a large share of crime, so holding those people longer removes a large share of harm.
Most people age out of crime on their own, so extra years are mostly served by people who would have stopped anyway, at great cost and for no safety gain.
Prison teaches criminal skills and cuts jobs and family ties, so people released after long terms often come out more dangerous than they went in.
The money spent on extra years of prison could pay for more officers on the street, and being likely to get caught deters more than the length of the sentence.
Police departments should spend more of their effort preventing crime than making arrests.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether harm that was prevented can be counted and answered for the way harm that was punished can.

text: An arrest happens after someone has already been hurt, while a visible patrol, better lighting, or a mediated dispute stops the harm before it occurs.
Arrests for minor offenses leave young people with a record that narrows their lawful paths and makes crime the easier one.
Communities share information with police who help them and hide it from police who mostly punish them, and that information is what solves serious crimes.
Prevention is hard to measure and easy to claim, while an arrest is a public act that can be checked, so shifting effort to prevention makes police less accountable.
People who have already been harmed are owed a response now, and putting arrests second means the department serves the person who might be hurt tomorrow ahead of the person who was hurt yesterday.
The surest form of prevention is the certainty that offenders get caught, and that certainty is built one arrest at a time.
Heavy digital editing generally does not make a photograph any less of a photograph.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether a photograph is defined by the camera's capture or by the finished picture the photographer chooses to show.

text: Every photograph already involves choices about framing, timing, lens and light, so editing afterward is one more choice among many rather than a break from the craft.
Printing and developing have always allowed the maker to lighten, darken, crop and combine, and nobody stopped calling those results photographs.
What viewers respond to is the finished image on the wall or the screen, and the tools used to reach it matter no more than the brand of brush matters for a painting.
Ordinary people trust a photograph because they assume it shows something that actually happened, and heavy editing quietly spends that trust without telling them.
A photograph's one special power over painting is its claim to have been there, so an image that no longer makes that claim has given up the thing that made it a photograph.

When any part of a picture can be changed after the camera has done its work, being in the right place at the right moment matters less than skill at software, and a photograph made that way is closer to an illustration than to a record.
A photograph's worth clearly rests more on what it truthfully shows than on the photographer's artistry.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether the camera's link to a real moment or the maker's eye is the source of a photograph's value.

text: The photographs people return to across generations are the ones that show something real, from a family's kitchen to a war, and their power comes from that reality rather than from technique.
Artistry can be produced on demand by anyone with training, but a true and telling moment cannot be staged without becoming something else.
When a striking image turns out to have been posed or altered, most people feel cheated, which shows that truth was what they valued all along.
Millions of truthful snapshots are taken every day and nearly all are forgettable, so truth alone plainly is not what separates a memorable image from a dull one.
Choosing where to stand, what to leave out and when to press the shutter is artistry, and it is what turns a scene anyone could see into a picture worth looking at.
Portraits, still lifes and fashion pictures are openly arranged, and they are among the most admired photographs ever made, which a truth-first view cannot explain.
Self-driving cars can clearly be made safer than human drivers on ordinary roads.
bottom_line: It comes down to whether the rare, strange situations a machine handles badly outweigh the common human failures it removes.

text: Most crashes come from distraction, tiredness, drunkenness and speeding, and a machine suffers from none of them.
A machine driver watches every direction at once and reacts faster than any person, so it can start braking or steering while a human is still noticing the danger.
When one automated car learns from a mistake, the fix goes to every car in the fleet, while every human driver has to learn each lesson alone.
Roads are full of unusual situations, from hand signals to fallen debris, and a system trained on typical cases fails exactly where judgment matters most.

On ordinary roads a self-driving car will need a human ready to take over for a long time, and a person told to supervise a machine stops paying attention, so the car plus its bored supervisor is more dangerous than a driver who knows the job is theirs.
Sensors fail in rain, snow, glare and dirt, and a driver who cannot see in bad weather is not safer than one who can.
Adding automation to critical systems tends to create new kinds of failure that are harder to catch than the ones it removes.
bottom_line: The disagreement is whether the surprising failures of automation are a permanent cost or a design problem that gets solved.

text: Automation hides what the system is doing, so when it fails the operators are surprised and have no time to understand what went wrong.
Operators who rarely act lose the skills they need in the moment the machine hands control back to them.
Automated parts are copied everywhere, so one hidden bug can fail in many places at once instead of one crew making one mistake.

A machine's possible failures are written into its rules and can be inspected and tested before it ever runs, while a person's failures come from mood, fatigue and distraction that nobody can inspect in advance, so the new failures are easier to catch, not harder.
Automated failures are logged and repeatable, so once they happen they can be found and fixed for good, while human lapses repeat forever.
The new failures automation creates can be designed against with alarms and backups, and every safety-critical industry has done so.
Free trade with other countries makes ordinary people in a country better off overall, even when some industries lose.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether small savings spread across every shopper outweigh heavy losses concentrated on particular towns and workers.

text: Buying goods from wherever they are made cheapest lowers prices for everyone, and lower prices raise living standards as surely as higher wages do.
Competition from abroad pushes home companies to improve and to focus on what they do best, which raises productivity across the economy.
Countries that trade heavily with each other have strong reasons to keep the peace, so trade buys security as well as cheaper goods.
The gains from trade are spread thinly across all consumers, while the losses land hard on particular towns and workers who rarely recover.
Depending on other countries for essential goods leaves a nation exposed when supply chains break or a trading partner turns hostile.
Trade deals let companies move production to places with weak labor and environmental rules, undercutting the protections workers at home fought for.
Public decisions should generally rest on measured statistics rather than on personal experience and anecdote.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether counting captures enough of what matters to be trusted over what people have lived through.

text: One person's experience covers a tiny slice of the world, and a count across many people is the only way to see the whole of it.
Anecdotes are remembered and repeated because they are striking, and striking cases are by definition unusual.
A number can be checked, repeated and argued about in the open, while a story cannot.
Statistics measure only what is easy to count, so relying on them pushes decisions toward whatever fits in a spreadsheet.
Averages hide the people at the edges, and the people at the edges are often the ones a decision hurts most.
Whoever chooses what gets counted and how shapes the answer before anyone sees the number, so a statistic carries the choices of its maker.
Statistics quoted in public debate tend to mislead more often than they inform.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether the misuse of numbers in debate outweighs the corrections that only numbers make possible.

text: A figure quoted without its definition, its source and its margin of error sounds precise while saying almost nothing.
Advocates pick the figure that helps their case from the many measures available, so the number the public hears is selected rather than representative.
Most readers cannot tell a sound statistic from a shaky one, so a shaky one carries the same authority as a sound one.
Most figures quoted in debate are roughly right, and the misleading ones stand out in memory precisely because they are the exception rather than the rule.
Misuse of statistics gets exposed by other statistics, which is exactly how public claims get corrected over time.
People are better at spotting a cherry-picked figure than critics assume, and the habit of asking where a number came from has spread.
Quoting a famous person generally adds little to whether a claim is true.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether the person behind a sentence is evidence for it or only an ornament on it.

text: A claim is true or false because of the reasons for it, and a name attached to it changes none of those reasons.
Famous people are quoted for saying things well, not for being right, and fine wording is not evidence.
Nearly any position can be backed by a quotation from someone famous, so quotations on opposite sides cancel each other out.
A quotation from a person with deep experience in a field is a compressed report of that experience, and experience is a kind of evidence.
A person whose judgment has proven sound on many past questions is more likely to be right on the next one, so a view held by such a person is more likely to be true, not merely more respectable.
A saying usually becomes famous by surviving years of public criticism from people who wanted it to be wrong, so a widely quoted claim has been tested in a way an anonymous claim has not.
Reference works should generally refuse to print a quotation whose original source cannot be found.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether an unverified saying is better printed with a label or left out altogether.

text: A saying passed on with the wrong name attached rewrites who thought what, and a reference work exists to prevent exactly that.
Misattributed quotations spread fastest once a respected reference repeats them, so the reference is the point where the chain can be broken.
Requiring a source forces editors to check the wording as well, and many well-known quotations turn out to have been reworded along the way.
Many sayings that shaped public life survive only in memory or in secondhand reports, and dropping them makes the reference less useful without making it more honest.
A quotation can be clearly labeled as attributed rather than confirmed, which gives readers the truth without throwing the entry away.
Insisting on a written original favors people whose words were recorded over those whose words were only spoken, which skews the record toward the already powerful.
Banks that are too big to fail should be broken up.
bottom_line: Whether the danger comes from a bank's size itself or from how much it is allowed to risk.

text: When a bank knows the government cannot let it fail, it can take bigger risks with other people's money and keep the winnings while taxpayers cover the losses.
Smaller banks can fail without dragging down the whole economy, which lets the market punish bad lending the way it should.
A handful of giant banks holds enormous sway over lawmakers and regulators, and breaking them up spreads that power out.
Large banks can fund large projects and serve customers across the world in ways that a collection of small banks cannot match.
Many small banks failing at the same time can cause a crisis just as easily as one big bank failing, so size is not the real problem.
Requiring big banks to hold more of their own capital and to keep plans for an orderly shutdown addresses the danger of a taxpayer bailout directly, without the disruption of forcing banks apart.
Rules that bar ordinary people from buying investments that are open to the wealthy do more harm than good.
bottom_line: Whether an adult's right to take a financial risk outweighs how easily the people selling that risk can take advantage of them.

text: Restricting the best early-stage investments to the already wealthy keeps the biggest gains in the hands of people who are already rich.
Adults are trusted to take on mortgages, start businesses and gamble at casinos, so it is inconsistent to say they cannot judge an investment.
Rules that keep ordinary people out of regulated investments push them toward unregulated corners of the market where they get less protection, not more.
Complex investments are designed by professionals who understand them far better than the buyer, and that gap is exactly where people get fleeced.
When ordinary savers lose their retirement money, the cost falls on public programs and families, not just on the person who took the risk.
Sellers of risky products have every incentive to push them hard, and a rule about who may buy is the simplest way to blunt that pressure.
Companies should be banned from putting forced arbitration clauses in consumer contracts.
bottom_line: Whether arbitration is a cheaper path to justice for consumers or a way for companies to avoid being held to account in public.

text: Nobody reads or negotiates the fine print on a phone plan or a bank account, so a forced arbitration clause buried there is imposed rather than agreed to.
Arbitration is private, so a company that cheats many customers in the same way can settle each one quietly and never be exposed.
The company picks and pays the arbitration service and is a repeat customer, while the consumer appears once, and that tilts the outcome.
Court is slow and expensive, and for a small claim arbitration is often the only route a consumer can actually afford to use.
Without arbitration, companies face class action suits that mostly pay lawyers while each customer receives a coupon.
Forcing disputes into court instead of arbitration raises companies' legal costs, which get built into prices so every customer pays for the few who sue.
Warning labels and disclosure rules do little to change how people buy and add cost without much benefit.
bottom_line: Whether the problem is disclosure itself or how badly most disclosures are written.

text: When every product carries a warning, people stop reading any of them, so the labels cancel each other out.
Long disclosure documents are written by lawyers to protect the company, not to inform the buyer, and no ordinary person reads them.
Disclosure lets regulators claim they acted while leaving the harmful product on the shelf, which crowds out rules that would actually work.
Simple, well-designed labels do change behavior, and the failure of bad labels is a reason to design better ones rather than to abandon them.

Printing a label or posting a fact sheet costs a company almost nothing next to the harm done when people buy a product without knowing what is in it, so disclosure rules cost far less than they save.
Requiring companies to state facts plainly changes what they are willing to sell, because nobody wants to print an ugly truth on their own package.
Training AI on copyrighted work without permission should be against the law.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether a machine learning from a work is more like a person reading it or more like a company copying it.

text: Writers, artists and musicians made the work that AI systems learn from, and using it to build a product that competes with them, without asking or paying, is a form of taking.
Any other business that wanted to use a book or a song commercially would need a license, and AI companies should not get an exemption because they use a great deal at once.
A permission requirement creates a market where creators can be paid, which keeps people making the new work that future AI systems will need.
Learning from what others made is how every human artist and writer has ever worked, and reading a book to learn from it has never required permission.

AI models are built to learn general patterns rather than keep copies of the works they train on, and the rare case where a model repeats a passage is a flaw to fix, so treating pattern learning itself as copying stretches copyright into control over ideas.
Requiring a license for every item in a training set would make useful AI possible only for the few companies rich enough to pay, and would stall research everywhere else.
Governments should not hold back the spread of AI in workplaces in order to protect existing jobs.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether slowing a technology to protect jobs actually saves workers or only delays the same change while the benefits go elsewhere.

text: Every major technology, from the tractor to the spreadsheet, was predicted to cause mass joblessness, and each time new kinds of work appeared instead, so a government that protects today's jobs is protecting jobs that would have changed anyway.
Most jobs are bundles of many tasks, and letting AI take over some of those tasks tends to change a job rather than end it, so there is far less to protect than the fear suggests.
Holding back AI in one country does not stop it anywhere else; the new jobs built around the tools simply grow abroad, and the protected jobs still disappear when cheaper foreign products arrive.

Past machines replaced muscle and left the thinking to people; a machine that can think is a different kind of thing, and a government that waits to see whether the old pattern holds risks finding out too late to help anyone.

Even when new jobs eventually appear, the people who lose the old ones are rarely the people who get the new ones, and slowing the change gives those workers time to retrain or retire before their livelihood is gone.

The spread of AI into workplaces is arriving faster than earlier shifts did, and a pace set by companies racing one another leaves schools, workers and towns no time to adjust unless government slows it down.
Governments should generally provide limited public funding to local newspapers so that local government keeps getting covered.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether a paper can watch a government that helps pay its bills, and whether readers walking away is a verdict on the product or a failure of the market.

text: When a town loses its paper, almost nobody attends council or school board meetings anymore, so local spending, contracts, and hiring go unwatched.
Newspapers did not lose readers so much as they lost advertisers, whose money moved to online platforms, so public money would replace lost revenue rather than reward bad reporting.
Societies already fund libraries, public schools, and courts because markets alone underprovide them, and local reporting belongs in that same category.
A newspaper that depends on government money cannot be trusted to cover that government as hard as it should, and readers will assume it does not.
Money should follow readers, and if not enough readers will pay for a paper, that shows it no longer meets a need people actually have.
Public funding programs for news tend to be captured by large chains with lobbyists, so the small local outlets those programs are meant to save get the least of the money.
A newspaper that can no longer pay its own way should generally be allowed to close rather than be kept alive with public money or special rules.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether a closing paper is a failed business that has served its time or a shared resource that nothing else replaces once it is gone.

text: Readers who stop paying for a paper are telling it something, and shielding it from that message keeps alive a product that no longer serves the people it claims to serve.
Money and talent tied up in a failing paper cannot flow to the newsletters, local news sites, and community radio that are already finding new ways to reach readers.
Once officials decide which papers get rescued, they are picking which voices survive, and a paper that owes its existence to that choice cannot report on those officials freely.

A town paper is not like a shoe store; when it closes, nothing else shows up to sit through zoning hearings and read the budget, so the loss lands on everyone, including people who never bought a copy.
Advertisers left for online platforms while readers still wanted local news, so letting a local paper die punishes the reporting for a problem in how it was paid for.

When a newsroom closes, its archive, its trained reporters, and its knowledge of the town scatter and do not come back when times improve, so a rescue can save something that is otherwise lost for good.
Cities that spend public money on stadiums for professional teams generally get back less than they put in.
bottom_line: It turns on whether money spent at a stadium is new money for the city or money residents would have spent somewhere else in town anyway.

text: Most of the money fans spend at a stadium is money they would otherwise have spent at local restaurants, theaters and shops, so the city gains little that is new.
Team owners keep most of the ticket, parking and concession income through favorable leases, while the public carries the construction debt for decades.
Owners of professional teams can threaten to move the team to another city, which forces cities to bid against each other and hand over far more than the team is worth to them.
A stadium can anchor development in a neglected district, drawing hotels, housing and restaurants that would not have come on their own.
The civic pride and shared identity a home team gives a city are a real return on public stadium spending, and comparisons that count only dollars leave that return out.
The construction jobs, game-day jobs and out-of-town visitor spending a new stadium brings can return as much to a city as the public money it put into the stadium.
Youth leagues should not offer tackle football to children below high school age.
bottom_line: It turns on whether the long-term harm from repeated head hits in childhood is large enough to override a family's right to choose.

text: A child's brain is still developing, and the damage from repeated head hits in tackle football builds up over years, so the earliest hits are the costliest ones.
A young child cannot weigh the risk of brain damage from tackle football, because that harm will not show up until middle age, so adults who will never bear it are making the choice for the child.

Flag football teaches the same footwork, routes and teamwork as tackle football without the collisions, so a child who waits until high school to start tackling misses nothing essential about the sport.

Parents already weigh serious injury risks when they let children ride bikes, ski or play soccer, and tackle football belongs in that same set of family decisions rather than under a league-wide rule.
Learning to tackle while bodies are small and slow teaches safe technique before players grow big enough to do real damage to each other.

Many children who want to play tackle football drop out of the sport when youth leagues offer only flag football, and the fitness and discipline they lose while waiting for high school are real costs.
Hunting is generally good for wildlife conservation.
bottom_line: It turns on whether wildlife is better protected by people who pay to hunt it or by managing land for its own sake.

text: License fees and taxes on hunting gear pay for much of the habitat protection and wildlife management that non-hunters enjoy for free.
Where wolves and other natural predators are gone, hunters keep deer and similar animals from overrunning forests and starving in bad winters.
People who hunt spend their lives outdoors and develop a personal interest in keeping land wild and undeveloped.
Managing land to please hunters keeps game animals artificially plentiful and shapes whole landscapes around a few species at the expense of the rest.

Because hunters want plentiful game, wildlife agencies that depend on them are pushed to shoot, trap and poison the wolves, cougars and coyotes that compete for it, which blocks the return of the natural predators a healthy ecosystem needs.
Trophy hunting takes the biggest and healthiest animals out of a population, which is the opposite of what natural selection would do.
Popular national parks should generally require timed-entry reservations.
bottom_line: It turns on whether a reservation protects the park experience or fences public land off from the people it belongs to.

text: Capping how many people are inside a popular national park at once keeps crowds from trampling trails, eroding fragile ground and driving wildlife away from its feeding and nesting areas.
Timed-entry reservations at national parks spread visitors across hours and days, so each person who enters gets the quiet and space they came for.
Timed-entry reservations at national parks replace hours of idling in car lines at the entrance with a set arrival time, so visitors lose less of their vacation to waiting.
National park reservation systems favor people with flexible schedules, fast internet and the habit of planning months ahead, and shut out working families and spontaneous travelers.
National parks are public land that belongs to every citizen, and a reservation system that turns some of them away at the entrance undermines the promise on which the parks were built.
Crowded national parks can add shuttles, parking and trails to handle more people rather than treating the number of visitors as the problem.

For most people, staying able-bodied into old age requires planned strength training that gets harder over time, because everyday activity alone is unlikely to preserve the muscle and bone that keep people independent.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether the muscle and bone lost with age can be kept by the loads of everyday life or only by loads deliberately made heavier than everyday life.

text: Muscle and bone grow stronger mainly when they face loads heavier than they are used to, so carrying groceries or climbing stairs can slow the loss at best but does little to build back what age takes away.

What ends independence is usually a fall or the inability to get up from a chair, and both come down to leg strength and balance, which improve most reliably when someone works against resistance on purpose.
Effort has to be measured to be kept up; without a plan that tracks what was lifted, exertion tends to drift down to whatever feels comfortable, which is the level that lets decline continue.

People in physically demanding jobs and in communities where everyone walks and carries often stay strong and mobile into very old age without ever following a program, which shows that a life full of physical work can be enough.
The body keeps what it uses, so a person who keeps gardening, carrying, climbing stairs and getting up off the floor keeps the strength for those exact tasks, and those are the tasks that matter.
A demanding program is quit far more often than it is kept, and strength that lasts a season and then stops does less for old age than modest activity kept up for a lifetime.
For most people, ordinary daily activity such as walking delivers most of the health benefit of exercise, and formal workouts add little.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether health gains from exercise level off after a modest amount or keep rising with more effort.

text: The biggest jump in health comes from going from doing nothing to doing something; the gain from doing more after that is much smaller.
People who build movement into their day, by walking to errands and taking stairs, keep it up for decades, while gym plans are usually abandoned.
Hard training carries injury risk and time cost that a brisk walk does not, and for most people those costs eat much of the benefit.
Walking can slow some loss of leg muscle, but it does little to build muscle back or to strengthen bone, and losing both is what leaves older people frail.
The benefits of fitness keep growing with more effort; people in the best shape live longer and healthier than the merely active.

Walking can be a real workout for the heart and lungs of someone who is out of shape, but as fitness improves an ordinary pace stops being hard, so the heart benefit levels off unless the effort goes up.
Doctors should generally follow standardized treatment guidelines rather than rely on their own judgment.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether the average patient is better served by the best evidence applied uniformly or by a doctor free to depart from it.

text: No single doctor can keep up with the research on every condition they treat, while a guideline distills the judgment of many specialists reviewing all the evidence.
Doctors given free rein vary enormously in what they prescribe for the same patient, and much of that variation is habit rather than reasoning.
A shared standard makes it possible to see which doctors and hospitals are getting worse results and to fix it.
Guidelines are written for the average patient, and the person in the exam room is never average; they have other conditions, other medicines, and their own goals.
A guideline is a snapshot of the evidence when it was written and can lag years behind what good doctors already know.
Following a treatment guideline step by step turns a physician into a technician and dulls the judgment needed for the cases the guideline did not anticipate.
Patients with serious illness should generally be free to try unproven treatments with their own money.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether a gravely ill person's right to take risks with their own body outweighs the risk of exploitation and of slower answers from clinical trials.

text: A person facing a grave illness has more at stake than any regulator, and deciding what risks to take with one's own body is the most basic freedom there is.
The approval process takes years, and patients who cannot wait deserve a chance at treatments that may work even if the proof is not yet complete.
Allowing informed patients to try new treatments produces experience that speeds up learning about what works.
Desperate people are the easiest to sell to, and freedom to try unproven treatments is in practice freedom for sellers to profit from false hope.
Unproven treatments can shorten life or add suffering, and a patient who spends savings and final months on one loses the chance at proven care and comfort.
If patients can get an experimental drug without joining a trial, fewer will join trials, and the answer about whether it works arrives later for everyone.
The highest-earning households should pay a larger share of their income in taxes than they do today.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether taking more from the rich mainly funds public goods or mainly drives money and jobs elsewhere.

text: A dollar taken from a very rich household changes nothing about how they live, while the same dollar taken from a working family means a bill goes unpaid.
Much of great wealth is built on public goods (courts that enforce contracts, roads, an educated workforce), and the people who gain most from them should pay most for them.
Concentrated wealth turns into concentrated political power, and a progressive tax is one of the few tools that limits that.
When a tax falls on a small group of top earners, most voters feel no cost from new spending, so government grows with nobody holding it in check.
High rates push wealthy people to move away, hide income, or shift it into forms that are taxed less, so the tax raises far less money than promised.
The rich are also the people most able to start and grow businesses, and taking more from them means fewer jobs for everyone else.
Sales taxes on everyday goods should be lower than they are today.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether fairness means everyone paying something or means the burden matching ability to pay.

text: Poor families spend nearly all their income, so a tax on spending taxes nearly everything they have, while rich families save much of theirs untouched by a sales tax.
A flat rate on spending draws no line between needs and wants unless lawmakers carve out exemptions, and where they have not, diapers are taxed like jewelry.
A high sales tax adds to the price of every purchase, so families buy less and local shops lose the sales they depend on.
Sales tax is the one tax nearly everyone pays, and a system where everyone contributes something is fairer than one where many pay nothing at all.
A sales tax is hard to avoid and cheap to collect, so it raises money reliably without the loopholes that plague income taxes.
Cutting sales taxes means either cutting the local services they fund (schools, roads, police) or raising some other tax, and there is no free option.
Scotland would be better off as an independent country.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether self-government is worth the economic and practical risks of leaving a long-standing union.

text: Scotland has repeatedly been governed by UK parties that most Scottish voters did not support, so decisions that shape Scottish life can go against Scotland's clear preference.
A Scottish government answering only to Scottish voters would be fully accountable for results, because it could no longer blame a distant parliament for choices it did not make.
Control over its own energy resources, immigration rules, and trade relationships would let Scotland shape its economy around its own strengths.
Independence would put a new national border between Scotland and England, its largest trading partner, and could disrupt the trade that many Scottish businesses depend on.
An independent Scotland would have a smaller tax base carrying services now funded from a shared United Kingdom pool, which means cuts or higher taxes.
Leaving the United Kingdom would mean Scotland rebuilding shared institutions, from pensions to defense to broadcasting, at great cost for uncertain gain.
The seven states that share the Colorado River should let the federal government decide how to divide its shrinking water supply rather than try to negotiate a deal among themselves.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether a decision imposed from outside would be more fair and workable than a deal the states reach themselves.

text: Each state that shares the Colorado River gains by holding out while the others give up water, so only an authority above all of them can make every state accept its fair share of the cuts.
Tribal nations, Mexico, and the river's wildlife all depend on the Colorado River but have no vote in a deal struck among states, and a federal decision can weigh their claims too.
The Colorado River supplies food and power that people across the whole country rely on, so how it is divided is a national question, not only a matter for the states along its banks.

Officials in the Colorado River states know their own farms, cities, and water rights far better than a distant federal agency, so a division decreed from the nation's capital is likely to get the details wrong.
A federal division of Colorado River water would be fought in court for years, and the river's users cannot wait that long for rules they can plan around.

When the Colorado River states write their own deal, water users can trade and share water among themselves, such as cities paying farmers to leave fields dry in drought years, which a top-down federal formula would make harder.
Charging drivers a fee to enter the most crowded part of Manhattan is the right policy.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether the fee is a fair price for scarce street space or a new cost on people and businesses that have no good way to avoid it.

text: Streets in central Manhattan are so jammed that buses, deliveries, and ambulances crawl, and a fee for driving into them is the most direct way to cut that traffic without banning anyone.
Money from a fee for driving into central Manhattan goes to the subway and bus system, so people who choose to drive help pay for the alternative that keeps everyone else moving.
Fewer cars entering central Manhattan mean cleaner air, less noise, and safer crossings in the neighborhoods that have suffered the most from through traffic.
A fee for driving into central Manhattan falls hardest on tradespeople, night-shift workers, and people from areas with poor transit who cannot simply switch to the train.
Drivers who want to avoid a fee for entering central Manhattan will park and idle in the neighborhoods just outside the charging zone, moving the traffic and pollution rather than removing it.
Shops, restaurants, and theaters in central Manhattan lose customers from the suburbs when driving in costs more, which hurts the owners and workers who depend on those visitors.
Houston is right to go without traditional citywide zoning.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether the lower prices and flexibility that come from letting land use sort itself out are worth giving up a public say over what gets built where.

text: Housing in Houston costs far less than in other big cities of similar size, and a main reason is that builders can put up homes where people want them without years of hearings.
Neighborhoods in Houston can change as the city changes, with shops, apartments, and houses mixing in ways that strictly zoned cities forbid.

Without citywide zoning, Houston officials have no rezoning decisions to hand out, which removes a common source of political favors, lobbying, and drawn-out neighborhood fights over each new project.

Without zoning to steer building away from low, flood-prone land around Houston, developers have paved areas that once soaked up rain, and everyone pays for the flooding that follows, not just the builders.

Without a citywide plan for where homes, offices, and industry will go, Houston struggles to put roads, drainage, and transit where growth is heading, so taxpayers end up paying to catch up after the fact.
Houston does not actually lack land-use rules; it relies on private deed restrictions that protect wealthier neighborhoods while leaving poorer ones exposed to whatever gets built next door.
A person's choices matter more than their circumstances in how their life turns out.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether the ability to choose well is itself something a person earns or something their circumstances hand them.

text: Siblings raised in the same home by the same parents often end up in very different places because they made different decisions about school, work, money, and friends, which shows that choices do much of the deciding.

People who receive a sudden windfall or suffer a sudden setback tend to drift back toward wherever their own habits were already taking them, so a change in circumstance changes the scenery but not the direction.
Small chosen habits, like showing up on time and finishing what you start, compound over years into most of the gap between people who thrive and people who do not.
The circumstances that matter most, such as where you were born, who raised you, and which school you attended, are settled before a person is old enough to choose anything.
The ability to make good choices is itself shaped by upbringing, stress, and example, so crediting the choice is crediting the circumstance in disguise.

The same mistake, like dropping out of school or taking on too much debt, is a short stumble for someone with a family safety net and a lasting disaster for someone without one, so how life turns out tracks the safety net more than the choice.
Most people's character is set by their upbringing and changes little in adulthood.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether the changes adults visibly make in their lives reflect a change in who they are or just a change in what they show.

text: Habits and instincts laid down in childhood are the hardest to unlearn because they were formed before anyone could question them.
Real change in an adult's character is rare and usually follows a major shock, and even then the core of the person, such as their temper and their outlook, tends to return once life settles down.
People choose friends, jobs, and places that confirm who they already are, so adult life mostly reinforces the character they arrived with.
People change jobs, faiths, politics, and partners across a lifetime, and their character moves with those changes in ways their parents would not recognize.
Adults keep learning new skills and dropping old fears, which shows the same capacity for change extends to temperament and values.

The traits that make up character, such as how careful, calm, and considerate a person is, keep shifting through the adult decades, and most people grow steadier and more patient with age rather than staying as they were at twenty.
Communities are generally better off when most people belong to a religious congregation.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether the good that congregations do comes from religion itself or from any close-knit group that meets every week.

text: A congregation gives people a regular reason to gather with neighbors across age, income, and background, which few other institutions still do.
Congregations carry a large share of the volunteer work, food drives, and care for the sick and grieving that towns quietly depend on.
A congregation gives neighbors a shared moral language that makes it easier to raise children, settle disputes, and trust one another without a contract.
Towns where most people belong to secular clubs, unions, and civic groups do just as well on trust and mutual help, so a town is no better off for having most people in congregations instead.
Congregations tend to draw a line around who belongs, and people on the wrong side of that line are often treated worse than in a town with no dominant faith.

When most residents belong to congregations, religious leaders gain quiet sway over local decisions, so questions like what the schools teach get settled by church teaching rather than by open public debate.
Religious beliefs should almost never be the basis for deciding what the law should be.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether laws need reasons that anyone can examine and check, or whether every moral view, religious or secular, rests on a starting point that cannot be proved.

text: Laws are enforced with fines and jail on people of every faith and of none, so it is unfair to punish someone for breaking a law whose only justification is a creed they do not share.
When the state backs one faith's rules, every other faith loses freedom, and the majority faith loses it too the moment it stops being the majority.
Religious arguments rest on revelation that evidence cannot check, so bringing them into lawmaking ends the debate instead of continuing it.

Many people's deepest moral convictions come from their faith, and asking them to leave those convictions out when they vote on laws or argue for them is asking them to take part in lawmaking as someone other than themselves.
Secular moral views about what the law should be also rest on assumptions no one can prove, so barring only religious reasons from lawmaking is not neutral but favors one worldview over another.

Many of the reform movements people now admire argued for changes in the law from faith, so a rule keeping religious reasons out of lawmaking would have shut out some of the most important legal reforms.
A four-year college degree is still worth its cost for most students.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether the average graduate's gains are large and reliable enough to justify the money and years that the below-average outcomes put at risk.

text: People with degrees tend to earn more over a working life than people without them, and that gap covers the cost of attending for most graduates.
Many careers with stable pay and good working conditions are closed to anyone without a degree, no matter how capable they are.
College teaches people to write, reason and work with strangers on hard problems, and those skills hold their value even when a specific job disappears.
Average college outcomes hide the many students who borrow heavily, never finish, and end up worse off than if they had never enrolled.
The earnings gap between degree holders and everyone else partly reflects who gets into college in the first place, so the degree itself deserves less credit than it usually gets.
Tuition has grown much faster than the wages a degree buys, so a calculation that once favored college no longer does for many majors and schools.
Most young people would be better served by trade training or an apprenticeship than by a four-year degree.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether the security of learning a trade today outweighs the wider range of doors a degree may open later in life.

text: Skilled trades pay well, are in short supply, and cannot be sent overseas or handed to software.
Apprentices earn while they learn instead of paying for four years and starting adult life in debt.
Many students sit through college courses they do not want because they were told there was no respectable alternative, and they would thrive doing hands-on work.
Trade work is often hard on the body, and workers who cannot continue in their forties or fifties have fewer ways to change careers than degree holders do.
A four-year degree is the entry ticket for graduate school, management and many licensed professions, and shutting that door at eighteen limits a person's whole life.
Pushing most young people toward trades would flood those fields and drive down the very wages that make them attractive now.
Letting public education money follow each student to the school their family chooses clearly improves education for the families who need it most.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether competition among schools lifts the whole system or mainly sorts students by which families are able to shop.

text: Wealthy families already choose schools by buying homes in good districts or paying tuition, and choice programs give poorer families the same power.
A school that must attract students has a reason to improve, while a school with a captive enrollment does not.
Children differ, and a system that lets a family match a child to a school's strengths serves that child better than one that assigns each child by address.

The families most able to shop for a school are also the ones who volunteer, raise money and push a school to fix its problems, so when they leave, the neighborhood school loses the people who held it to account.
Private schools that take public money can still turn students away, so the choice belongs to the school more than to the family.

A public school must answer to an elected board and open its records, so a family whose child is failed has a vote and a public process to use; when money moves to private schools that owe families neither, the families with the least time and money to fight for their children lose the tools they most rely on.
Sending public money to private and charter schools generally weakens the neighborhood schools that most children still attend.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether a student leaving takes away more in funding than the school saves in cost, and whether that loss lands on the students who stay.

text: Most of a school's costs, such as buildings, buses and staff, do not shrink when a few students leave, so each departure leaves less per remaining child.
Choice programs tend to draw the students who are cheapest to educate, leaving public schools a higher share of children with disabilities and language needs.

When many of the families with the most time and influence move their children to private or charter schools, fewer voters have a personal stake in the neighborhood schools, and support for their budgets and building repairs tends to fade.
A student who leaves takes funding with them, but the school also stops paying to teach that student, so the money left per child who stays does not have to fall.
A neighborhood school that loses students to a rival has a stronger reason to fix whatever drove them away, so competition tends to make it better rather than weaker.

Many neighborhood schools are crowded, so when some students leave for a private or charter school, the children who stay get smaller classes and more of each teacher's time, which leaves their school stronger rather than weaker.
Canceling a large share of existing student loan debt would do more good than harm.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether the relief to struggling borrowers outweighs the cost to everyone else and the signal it sends to future borrowers and schools.

text: Millions of people took on student loans as teenagers on the advice of parents, counselors and schools, and they should not carry a bad bet for decades.
Student loan payments delay home buying, starting families and starting businesses, and canceling that debt would free money that would ripple through the whole economy.
Government has absorbed losses or extended rescue terms to farms and corporations in hard times, and ordinary graduates deserve the same consideration.
Student loan forgiveness taxes people who never went to college, or who paid their loans off by living cheaply, to help people who on average earn more than they do.
Wiping out today's student debt does nothing about tomorrow's, and schools will keep raising prices if they learn the bill eventually lands elsewhere.
A one-time cancellation of student debt rewards those who borrowed the most, not those who need help the most, when targeted relief could reach the truly stuck.
Adults who borrowed for college generally should repay their loans rather than pass the cost to taxpayers who did not attend.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether a loan signed at eighteen under heavy pressure is a fair bargain that binds like any other contract.

text: A loan is a promise, and a society that erases promises when they become inconvenient makes every future promise worth less.
Borrowers chose their school and major, and the people who chose cheaper paths should not be billed for someone else's choice.
The fair fix for an unaffordable loan is a payment plan tied to income, which already exists, rather than shifting the whole balance to the public.
Teenagers cannot judge a loan whose terms depend on a job market a decade away, and it is not fair to hold them to a decision adults set up for them.
Public colleges were once cheap because taxpayers funded them, and the shift to student loans was itself a decision to bill the young for what older generations got at a heavily subsidized price.
Interest that grows faster than a graduate can pay turns a fixed debt into a lifelong one, which few borrowers understood they were agreeing to.
Schools should generally require students to read the classic works of literature rather than let them choose their own books.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether the main job of school reading is to hand down a shared inheritance or to build a lasting habit of reading.

text: A society needs stories and phrases that everyone recognizes, and required reading is the surest way to give a whole generation the same set of older works to draw on.
Difficult books build the ability to read difficult things, and students who are only ever asked to read what comes easily never develop that strength.
Students cannot choose a book they have never heard of, so leaving the choice to them mostly means leaving it to whatever is already popular and marketed to them.
Forcing teenagers through books they find dull is the most reliable way to convince them that reading is a chore, and many never pick up a book again once school ends.
The list of classics reflects who had the power to publish and to teach in earlier centuries, so treating it as the measure of greatness passes on those old exclusions.
Reading skill grows mainly from the sheer amount a person reads, and students read far more when they are allowed to follow their own interests.
Popular genre fiction such as romance, crime and fantasy generally deserves the same critical respect as literary fiction.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether the line between literary and genre fiction marks a real difference in ambition or only a difference in shelving and prestige.

text: Plotting, pacing, character and sentence craft are the same skills whichever shelf a book sits on, and a well-made thriller demands as much of them as a well-made literary novel.
The split between literary and genre fiction is a marketing label invented by publishers and prize committees, not a quality that can be found inside the books themselves.
Many books now taught as classics were written as popular entertainment in their day, which suggests that today's genre fiction will supply some of tomorrow's classics.
Literary fiction is defined by taking risks with form, language and moral ambiguity, and genre conventions exist precisely to limit those risks so that readers get what they expect.

A book written mainly to entertain succeeds by delivering pleasure, while a book written to explore human experience succeeds by what it reveals, so granting both the same critical respect ignores that they are attempting different and unequally demanding things.

Serious review space and prize attention are scarce, and spending them on books that already have large and loyal readerships takes them away from the ambitious books that need a critic's help to find any readers at all.
Philosophy should generally be taught in high school alongside math and science.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether teenagers can be taught to reason through hard questions in a classroom or whether the subject needs a maturity and training most schools cannot supply.

text: Philosophy teaches how to tell a good argument from a bad one and how to disagree without fighting, and those skills are needed by every citizen in every job.
Teenagers already face questions about fairness, honesty, free will and what makes a life worth living, and school currently leaves them to work these out from whatever they find online.
Every other subject rests on assumptions about what counts as knowledge and why it matters, and philosophy is the one place a student gets to examine those assumptions directly.
The school day is already full, and adding philosophy means cutting time from reading, math or science, where students have measurable needs that are not being met.

Most teenagers lack the background knowledge and patience philosophy demands, so a high school philosophy class tends to become a discussion of opinions in which nobody learns anything they did not already believe.
Few teachers are trained to teach philosophy well, and a badly taught philosophy course is worse than none, because it convinces students the subject is empty talk.
Philosophy generally makes no real progress on its big questions.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on what should count as progress when the questions themselves never get closed the way scientific questions do.

text: The same questions about free will, the nature of goodness and what we can know have been argued for as long as philosophy has existed, and there is still no agreed answer to any of them.
Philosophy has no shared method for settling a dispute, so rival schools can persist side by side for centuries with no way to show that one of them has been proven wrong.

Whenever a philosophical question does get answered, it stops being called philosophy and becomes physics, psychology or economics, which leaves philosophy holding only the questions that cannot be settled.
Progress in philosophy takes the form of ruling out answers that once seemed plausible and sharpening the questions, and by that measure the field is far ahead of where it started.

Careful arguments about who deserves fair treatment and whose suffering counts have changed what most people believe is right and wrong, and a widely shared answer to part of an ancient question about goodness is real progress on that question.

Parts of the old big questions, such as how the mind works and what the world is made of, moved into science only after philosophers made them precise enough to test, so that move shows philosophy advancing its questions rather than failing at them.
Human activity is clearly the main cause of the warming seen over the past century.
bottom_line: It turns on whether the match between rising gases and rising temperatures rules out natural swings that are known to occur.

text: Global warming over the past century closely tracks the rise in heat-trapping gases from burning coal, oil and gas, and no natural cause matches its timing.
Scientists have measured in laboratories for generations how carbon dioxide and other heat-trapping gases absorb heat, so warming from adding more of them to the air is expected, not a surprise.
The pattern of recent warming, with Earth's lower atmosphere warming while its upper atmosphere cools, is the signature of heat trapped by gases and not of a brighter sun.
Earth's climate has swung between warm and cold periods long before industry, so a warm stretch on its own is not proof of a human cause.

Temperature records need large adjustments for station moves, instrument changes and gaps, so the close match between rising gases and rising temperatures may be sensitive to those adjustment choices.
Ocean cycles run for decades and can add to or hide warming, making it hard to separate the human share of recent global warming from natural swings.
Scientists and agencies who publish regional and local climate forecasts generally present them with more confidence than the climate models behind them have earned.
bottom_line: The dispute is really about whether the disagreement between climate models is honestly carried through to the local forecasts people act on.

text: Climate models agree about warming for the planet as a whole but disagree sharply about future rainfall and storms in any single region, so a local forecast built from one model or one average hides that disagreement.

Climate models divide the world into boxes many miles wide, so clouds and rainstorms smaller than one box are estimated with rough rules rather than directly simulated, which makes local rainfall forecasts less certain than they look.

Many local climate forecasts are made by scaling down global climate models with statistical shortcuts, and those shortcuts add errors of their own that are rarely shown to the people using the forecasts.
Official regional climate projections are usually published with ranges and several scenarios, and planners are told to use the full range, so the uncertainty is disclosed rather than hidden.

Climate models forecast some regional shifts, such as the Arctic warming faster than the rest of the world, before those shifts showed up clearly in local records, so regional climate projections have some track record behind them.

Many regional climate projections rest on simple physics that does not depend on fine detail, such as land warming faster than sea and warmer air holding more moisture, so confidence in those projections is earned even where small-scale details are rough.
String theory has clearly failed to earn the central place it holds in physics.
bottom_line: It comes down to whether a theory can earn its place through mathematical power alone or only through a prediction that could fail.

text: A theory that fits any possible observation explains nothing, and string theory allows so many versions that it can be made to fit almost anything.
A theory earns its place by explaining something older theories could not, and string theory has not yet explained any measured quantity that physicists could not already account for.
The new partner particles that many versions of string theory expected at high energies have not shown up in experiments, which weakens the case that was built on them.
String theory is the most developed approach that fits gravity and quantum physics into one framework, and that achievement alone justifies its place while rivals remain less complete.
Many accepted theories waited generations for the technology to test them, so string theory's lack of a test today is not proof of failure.
String theory's mathematics has already solved problems in other fields, which shows it is productive even before any direct test.
Building a new, larger particle collider is clearly worth its cost for what it could reveal.
bottom_line: The question is whether reaching higher energy is guaranteed to teach something, or is a bet with no theory saying what is there.

text: Every jump in collision energy has found new particles or ruled out ideas, and there is no other way to probe matter at those scales.
The technology built for particle colliders, from magnets to data handling, tends to spread into medicine and computing, so part of the value comes back even if no new particle is found.
Spread over decades and many countries, the cost of a new, larger particle collider is small against national budgets and buys an experiment no single nation could do alone.
The last big particle collider found what was expected and nothing beyond it, and no theory says a larger one will reach anything new.
The money for a new particle collider could instead fund many smaller experiments across many fields, which together offer more chances of a surprise.
Precise measurements of known particles and cheaper sky-watching experiments can test the ideas a new collider would test, without building a new machine.
Governments should generally fund efforts to keep endangered minority languages alive.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether a language can be kept alive by public programs at all, or only by families who choose to speak it at home.

text: A language carries a community's stories, humor, and ways of seeing the world that cannot be fully translated, and because losing it is a loss for everyone, the public has good reason to pay to prevent it.
Many minority languages were pushed toward extinction by past government policy, so public money to reverse that is fair repair rather than a favor.

Children who keep their home language while learning the national one tend to do better in school, not worse, so public funding of minority-language programs helps the very students it is meant to serve.
Public money is limited, and paying to keep alive a language few people choose to speak takes funds from schools and services that reach far more people.
Languages survive mainly when parents speak them to their children at home, and publicly funded classes rarely lead families to do that, so the money seldom achieves what it is meant to.
Publicly funded programs that teach children in a minority language take school hours away from the national language, which can leave those children less fluent in the language most jobs require.
Schools in a country with one dominant language should teach mainly in that language rather than in students' home languages.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether children learn the dominant language faster by being immersed in it or by first becoming strong readers in a language they already understand.

text: Sharing one language lets citizens argue, vote, and work together, and school is the main place that shared language is built.
Students who spend most of the school day in the dominant language reach fluency faster, which is what they need for college and jobs.
Running classes in many home languages is expensive and hard to staff, so in practice it means worse teaching for the students it is meant to help.
Children learn to read and do math faster in a language they already understand, and those skills carry over once they learn the dominant language.

Making the dominant language the main language of instruction signals to children that their family's language matters less, which can hurt their confidence and weaken ties with parents and grandparents.

Children taught partly in their home language keep it and grow into fully bilingual adults, while schooling mainly in the dominant language tends to replace the home language and throw away a skill that helps in trade, diplomacy, and many jobs.
Where a person ends up in life is shaped more by the family and neighborhood they were born into than by their own choices.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether the choices people make are truly their own or are themselves largely produced by the circumstances they were born into.

text: A child's schooling, health, safety, and connections are set before they can make any choices, and those early conditions shape which choices are later available.
People born into wealth who make poor choices usually land softly, while people born poor who make good choices often still struggle, which shows circumstance outweighs choice.
The habits and expectations people call choices are largely learned from the people around them, so choice itself is a product of circumstance.

Brothers and sisters raised in the same home by the same parents often end up in very different places as adults, and the gaps between them regularly line up with the decisions each one made about school, work, and friends, which a shared upbringing cannot explain.

Early conditions set the starting line rather than the finish, because habits built in adulthood, such as showing up, saving, and staying out of trouble, compound over decades in ways that birth circumstances do not.
Immigrants who arrive with nothing and rise within a generation show that steady work and patience can overcome the disadvantages of a poor starting point.
In wealthy countries, most adults who stay poor do so mainly because of their own choices about school, work, and family, not because the chance to escape was closed to them.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether the choices that separate people who stay poor from people who escape are genuinely open to almost everyone or are mostly shaped by the advantages people start with.

text: In wealthy countries, free public schooling and widely available entry-level jobs mean that most young adults, even those raised poor, have a real chance to finish school and start earning.

A household with two committed adults has two incomes and two people's time to absorb a lost job or a sick child, so deciding to marry before having children protects a family from hardship that a single parent often cannot escape.

Many people who grow up poor leave poverty as adults while others from the same background do not, and the difference usually tracks decisions such as dropping out of school, quitting jobs, or having children early.

People who finish school, keep steady work, and marry before having children usually had supportive families and safe neighborhoods to begin with, so those habits reflect advantages they were given rather than choices that explain their success.
In places where steady jobs have disappeared, full-time work often does not pay enough to lift a family out of poverty, so people there stay poor even when they make every sensible choice.

Marrying before having children depends on finding a partner with a steady income, and in communities where such partners are scarce, that path is not really open to people no matter what they choose.
Dictionaries should generally record how people actually use words rather than rule on which uses are correct.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether a dictionary's job is to report the language as it is or to guide it toward what it should be.

text: Language changes whether or not anyone approves of the change, so a dictionary that refuses to record a common meaning stops describing the language people speak.
Readers open a dictionary to find out what a word they just met means, and that need is met only if the entry covers the meanings in real use.
No group of editors has the authority to decide for millions of speakers what their own words mean.
A dictionary is one of the few tools that lets writers agree on a shared standard, and giving up that role leaves nobody to hold the line.
Listing a widespread use that began as an error, without marking it as disputed, speeds the loss of useful distinctions between words.

An entry that records how a word is used without saying how careful writers and educated readers will receive that use leaves students and people learning the language without the guidance they most need.
A dictionary should generally refuse to list a widespread misuse of a word as a legitimate meaning until careful writers have accepted it.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether a meaning becomes real once enough people use it or only once careful writers accept it.

text: When a dictionary lists a common mistake as a meaning, readers take the entry as permission to use it, so the dictionary itself speeds the spread of the error.
A dictionary earns its authority by being selective, and an entry that treats a misreading as a settled meaning spends that authority on a fashion that may not last.
Waiting until careful writers accept a new meaning costs little, because a use that truly enters the language will still be there when the dictionary catches up.
Which uses of a word count as misuses depends on who is asked, so waiting for careful writers to approve a meaning hands a small group control over what a whole language is allowed to mean.
A reader who meets a word in a common but disputed sense and cannot find that sense in the dictionary is left worse informed, which defeats the reason the dictionary exists.
Treating a widespread use of a word as an error mostly stigmatizes the speech of particular regions and social classes, and a reference work should not do that.
Television channels that present opinion shows in the style of a newscast should be required to label those shows as opinion on screen.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether a government can draw the line between news and opinion without also deciding what counts as news.

text: When an opinion host sits at the same desk, with the same graphics and the same tone as the news anchor, most viewers cannot tell which one they are watching.

Printed newspapers have kept opinion on a labeled editorial page, apart from the news pages, for generations, so requiring an on-screen opinion label on television asks channels to do only what print has long done.

When viewers mistake a television commentator's argument for reported fact, they come away sure of things no reporter has checked, and that confusion wears down trust in the real reporting on the same channel.
Any official body that decides which segments are opinion is deciding which segments are news, and that is a power no government should hold over the press.
Every honest newscast contains analysis, framing, and judgment calls, so the line between news and opinion that an on-screen labeling rule would have to draw does not exist in practice.
Regular viewers of television news already know which hosts are commentators and which are reporters, so an on-screen opinion label would tell them nothing they do not already know.
Publicly funded television news is generally not worth the cost now that viewers have countless free sources.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on whether having many sources is the same as having a reliable one, and whether a channel free of advertising pressure is a different product or just a subsidized one.

text: Taxpayers pay for a public news channel most of them never watch, while the people who do watch it could afford to pay for it themselves.
Public broadcasters tend to reflect the tastes and assumptions of the educated professionals who run them, so the public pays for a channel that speaks for a slice of it.
A news outlet that depends on government money has its budget set by the officials it is supposed to cover, so it is never fully free to report on them.

Because a publicly funded news channel does not depend on advertisers, it has no reason to chase outrage the way commercial channels do, so it offers viewers something the free commercial channels do not.

Publicly funded television news covers the stories commercial channels skip because they draw few viewers, such as state legislatures, local government meetings, and slow investigative reporting that takes months to finish.
When people face countless news sources of uneven quality, a publicly funded broadcaster with a duty to be accurate gives them one trusted reference point against which to check the rest.
Social media platforms should be required to pay news publishers for the articles that draw users into their feeds.
bottom_line: The disagreement turns on who is doing whom the favor: the platform sending readers to the publisher, or the publisher supplying the platform with something worth reading.

text: Social media platforms earn advertising money from posts built around news reporting they did not pay for, so the value created in the newsroom is collected somewhere else.
